concept.name: Bear steepener
concept.definition: A steepening of the yield curve driven by long-term interest rates rising faster than short-term rates. It is called 'bear' because rising yields mean falling bond prices, and the pattern often appears when inflation expectations pick up and the market anticipates tighter policy to follow.
concept.intuition: The curve steepens from the long end selling off: long rates rise (long bonds fall) faster than short rates.
concept.mechanics: Classified by decomposing the spread change: the long-end yield rises faster than the front-end yield, widening the spread. A steepener position (long front leg, short back leg) gains; the short back leg captures most of the move because the long end drives the steepening.
concept.formula: Condition: Δy_long > 0 and Δ(y_long - y_short) > 0, i.e. the back-end yield rises faster than the front-end yield.
concept.failure_modes: Descriptive, not predictive: bear steepeners can reverse violently on flight-to-safety rallies that hit the long end hardest. Inflation-driven steepening may also be accompanied by rising real yields that pressure the same risk assets the trader holds elsewhere.
concept.misconceptions: It does not mean short rates are static — they may also rise, just less. Nor does a bear steepener necessarily signal imminent Fed hikes; it can reflect rising term premium or supply concerns in long-dated issuance.
concept.example: The 10-year yield rises from 4.0% to 4.6% on inflation fears while the 2-year rises only from 4.5% to 4.7%; the 2s10s spread widens from -50 bp to -10 bp — a bear steepener.

citations.source: LearnBonds: Bull Flattener, Bear Flattener, Bull Steepener and Bear Steepener Explained
